questions.q: What is the main role of the proteins “53BP1, RIF1 and Shieldin” in DNA repair?
options: Forming a protective structure at the DNA ends so that DNA polymerase can extend
Patrolling the whole chromosome to recognise the damaged DNA segment
Preventing the DNA ends from being resected, so that the double-strand break is left for NHEJ to join
Pairing two homologous chromosomes together as a template for recombination
questions.why: These proteins inhibit DNA end resection, leaving the ends of the double-strand break intact for NHEJ; once the ends have been cut away, the cell can only fall back on the HR route. The other choices describe a protective structure that lets DNA polymerase extend, a protein patrolling the chromosome for damaged segments, and the pairing of homologous chromosomes as a recombination template.

questions.q: The cell attaches an alkyl group to a DNA base, so that the chemical properties of the base are changed; what is this type of DNA damage called?
options: Alkylation
Polymerase slippage
Direct reversal
Radiation
questions.why: Alkylation is one way of chemically changing a base (for example the methyl group that MGMT removes); slippage is slipping during replication, direct reversal puts the altered base back the way it was, and radiation causes double-strand breaks.

questions.q: Which way of repairing a double-strand break does “alternative end joining (a-EJ)” describe?
options: High-fidelity repair that uses the sister chromatid as a template and runs in S/G2
Excising a single damaged base and having DNA polymerase put back the correct base
Excising a stretch of 22–32 nucleotides so that a bulky lesion is removed in its entirety
An alternative end-joining pathway that does not depend on Ku and needs no template, and often ends in large deletions
questions.why: a-EJ is an end-joining pathway other than NHEJ: it needs no template and does not depend on Ku, but because it is imprecise it often causes large deletions. The other choices are HR, BER and NER.

questions.q: After an antigen-presenting cell has processed the antigen into peptides, which molecule mainly displays those peptides on the cell surface for T cells to recognise?
options: TCR (T-cell receptor)
MHC (major histocompatibility complex)
V(D)J recombination
Mismatch repair (MMR)
questions.why: MHC is the presenting side: class I presents to CD8 and class II to CD4; TCR is the receiving side, while V(D)J recombination and MMR belong to immune diversity and DNA repair respectively.

questions.q: After DNA glycosylase has cut out the damaged base, a position with no base at all is left in the DNA; this position is called ______.
options: Nucleotide excision repair (NER)
Mismatch repair (MMR)
AP site
Double-strand break (DSB)
questions.why: An AP site is the abasic site: once the base has been cut away the sugar–phosphate backbone is left behind and later enzymes put back the correct base — this is the scene after the first step of BER.

questions.q: What is the role of “ATM” in the DNA damage response?
options: A kinase that senses double-strand breaks and switches on downstream signalling (for example p53)
Patrolling the whole chromosome to recognise the damaged DNA segment
Sliding along DNA to localise the damage and assemble the excision enzymes there
Delivering the guide RNA to the DNA so that Cas9 can cut next to the PAM
questions.why: ATM senses double-strand breaks and switches on downstream signalling (for example p53). The other choices describe XPC (patrolling the chromosome and recognising damaged segments), XPA (sliding along DNA to localise the damage and assemble the excision enzymes), and the CRISPR targeting procedure, all of which have a different division of labour from ATM.

questions.q: When the cell meets a stalled replication fork during DNA replication, or single-stranded DNA appears on the DNA, which kinase is mainly responsible for sensing it and relaying the signal?
options: ATM
PARP inhibitor
ATR
questions.why: ATM senses double-strand breaks, whereas ATR senses replication-fork stalling and single-stranded DNA; the two are the most upstream sensing points of the DNA damage response.

questions.q: Which type of DNA damage does “Base excision repair (BER)” repair?
options: A bulky lesion spanning several nucleotides, for example the pyrimidine dimer caused by ultraviolet light
A single damaged base, for example one that has been alkylated or oxidised
A base that is mismatched between the newly synthesised strand and the old strand
Both strands of the DNA breaking at the same time
questions.why: BER touches only one base: DNA glycosylase first cuts it out to leave an AP site, and polymerase then puts the correct base back; bulky lesions are the business of NER, mismatches are MMR, and double-strand breaks are handled by HR or NHEJ.

questions.q: During homologous recombination, the branched structure formed where two DNA single strands cross can move along the DNA; what is this step, which pushes the crossover point forward, called?
options: CA loop
recombination-signal sequences
branch migration
polymerase slippage
questions.why: Branch migration is an intermediate step of homologous recombination: the crossed branch moves along the DNA so that mismatches between the heteroduplex strands can be corrected; a CA loop, by contrast, is the looped structure formed when a protein slides along DNA.

questions.q: What is the most famous significance of “BRCA1 and BRCA2” in tumour biology?
options: Mutations disable homologous recombination (HR), so the tumour becomes especially sensitive to PARP inhibitors
Mutations disable NHEJ, causing severe immunodeficiency in the patient
Mutations disable mismatch repair, turning the tumour into an MSI-H hot tumour
Mutations disable nucleotide excision repair, so the dimers caused by ultraviolet light cannot be excised
questions.why: BRCA1/2 are important members of the HR machinery; once they lose function the cell has only the error-prone NHEJ left, so the damage caused by a PARP inhibitor cannot be repaired — this is the classic example of synthetic lethality. The other choices describe a loss of NHEJ causing severe immunodeficiency, a loss of mismatch repair producing an MSI-H hot tumour, and a loss of nucleotide excision repair leaving ultraviolet dimers in place.

questions.q: When a DNA repair protein slides along DNA and grips the double-stranded DNA, it pulls the DNA into a circular loop; what is this structure called?
options: PAM
RPA
Ku
CA loop
questions.why: A CA loop is the circular loop pulled out when a protein slides along DNA; it commonly appears in descriptions of how damage is searched for and located on DNA.

questions.q: When DNA damage is severe and cannot be repaired, the cell initiates apoptosis: the extrinsic pathway is started by caspase 8, while the mitochondrial intrinsic pathway is started by ______.
options: caspase 8
caspase 9
ATM
Ku
questions.why: Caspase 8 runs the extrinsic (death receptor) pathway and caspase 9 the mitochondrial intrinsic pathway; both are the starting points that turn irreversible damage into apoptosis.

questions.q: How does the “CRISPR/Cas9” gene-editing system work?
options: A protein recognises the DNA with zinc fingers and then two nucleases cut at the target site
mRNA is transcribed from a DNA template and a foreign sequence is inserted into the genome
An RNA carries Cas9 to the DNA, and Cas9 then cuts both strands next to the PAM
The sister chromatid is used as a template to swap out the entire target gene
questions.why: CRISPR/Cas9 uses gRNA to recognise the DNA and Cas9 to make the cut. Among the other choices, one is the ZFN approach — recognition by zinc fingers, which is far more expensive to design and has therefore been superseded; one is transcribing mRNA from a DNA template and inserting a foreign sequence into the genome; and one is the HR approach of using the sister chromatid as a template to swap out the entire target gene.

questions.q: In nucleotide excision repair (NER), which two genes are responsible for arranging the excision on the strand of DNA that is being transcribed?
options: CSA and CSB
XPC and XPA
XPF and XPG
ATM and ATR
questions.why: CSA and CSB belong to TC-NER: when the transcription complex stalls on damaged DNA it summons the repair machinery on the spot; XPC handles the genome-wide scan, XPF and XPG make the cuts, and ATM and ATR are the signal sensors.

questions.q: There is a class of DNA damage in which the cell excises nothing and instead puts the altered base back the way it was; what is this repair mode called?
options: Base excision repair (BER)
Nucleotide excision repair (NER)
Mismatch repair (MMR)
Direct reversal
questions.why: Direct reversal repairs without excising any DNA: for example MGMT simply removes the alkyl group from an alkylated base and the base stays in place; BER, NER and MMR all excise first and then resynthesise.

questions.q: The diversity of antibodies and T-cell receptors comes from combining three kinds of gene segment, V, D and J; in chapter 6 this diversity is called ______.
options: Homologous recombination (HR)
Diversity
Mismatch repair (MMR)
Direct reversal
questions.why: The figures the lecturer gives are V ≈ 39 copies, D = 27 and J = 6, which combine to give receptor diversity; because V(D)J recombination borrows NHEJ, an NHEJ defect means this diversity can never be built up.

questions.q: What does a “DNA adduct” mean?
options: A complex formed by a protein binding to DNA
The hydrogen bonds between two complementary bases in DNA
An adduct formed when a chemical carcinogen or drug binds covalently to a DNA base
A duplex molecule formed by RNA hybridising with DNA
questions.why: A DNA adduct is the product formed when a chemical carcinogen (for example NNK in tobacco smoke) is activated by hepatic P450 and then binds to a base; if the adduct is not repaired it is fixed as a mutation during replication. The other choices describe a protein–DNA complex, the hydrogen bonds between complementary bases, and an RNA–DNA hybrid duplex.

questions.q: After the cell detects DNA damage, the overall response that sets off a whole cascade of signalling and handling (halting the cell cycle, repairing, even apoptosis) is called what?
options: DNA Damage Response (DDR)
Effectors
Transducer
Direct reversal
questions.why: The DDR is the overall response: sensors detect the damage, transducers pass the signal on, and effectors carry out the response; these three stages are used to describe the chain. The other options are the last stage of the chain, the middle stage that passes the signal down, and a repair mode that excises nothing.

questions.q: The first enzyme to act in the BER pathway is DNA glycosylase: it cuts out the damaged base, leaving a ______ in the DNA, and later enzymes then put back the correct base.
options: Double-strand break (DSB)
Mismatch repair (MMR)
Nucleotide excision repair (NER)
AP site
questions.why: DNA glycosylase cuts only the base and not the sugar–phosphate backbone, leaving a base-less AP site behind; this is also the dividing line between BER and NER — NER cuts out the whole stretch of DNA that contains the bulky lesion.

questions.q: Chapter 6 divides the handling of DNA damage into: direct reversal, BER, NER, MMR, and, for double-strand breaks, ______ and NHEJ.
options: Base excision repair (BER)
Homologous recombination (HR)
Nucleotide excision repair (NER)
Mismatch repair (MMR)
questions.why: Only two pathways can join a double-strand break: HR, which uses a template, and NHEJ, which does not; HR is accurate but restricted to S/G2, whereas NHEJ works in every phase but is error-prone. The other choices are the pathways for a single damaged base, for bulky lesions and for replication mismatches.

questions.q: To make a targeted knock-in with CRISPR and insert a new stretch of DNA precisely into the target gene, what is the separately supplied DNA carrying the sequence to be inserted called?
options: gRNA
PAM
donor template
RuvC
questions.why: A knock-in needs a donor template for the insertion to be precise and site-specific; gRNA merely brings Cas9 to the site, PAM is the adjacent-sequence requirement for Cas9 to cut, and RuvC is Cas9's nuclease domain.

questions.q: In the chapter 6 classification, which damage is listed as the most severe and the one that has to be dealt with by pathways such as end joining or recombination?
options: DNA damage in which both strands are broken
A single base that has been alkylated
A pyrimidine dimer caused by ultraviolet light
A base mismatch in the newly synthesised strand once replication is complete
questions.why: A double-strand break is the most severe form and is sensed by ATM; there are only two ways to handle it — template-dependent HR and template-free NHEJ. The other choices are a single alkylated base, an ultraviolet pyrimidine dimer and a mismatch left in the newly synthesised strand after replication.

questions.q: In the signalling chain of the DNA damage response, which kind of molecule is meant by “Effectors”?
options: Sensor proteins that detect the damage and emit the first signal
Proteins that slide along DNA to position the repair machinery at the damaged site
Receptors that convert an external stimulus into an intracellular signal
Working molecules at the end of the signalling chain that actually carry out the repair or decide the cell's fate
questions.why: The damage response is described in three stages, sensors → transducers → effectors: the sensors detect the damage, the signal is passed downwards, and the effectors finally decide whether to repair, to arrest, or to undergo apoptosis. The other choices describe the sensors at the start of the chain, the proteins that position the repair machinery, and the receptors that convert an external stimulus into an intracellular signal.

questions.q: If DNA mutagens are classified by source, the endogenous ones come from replication errors and ______; ultraviolet light and ionising radiation, by contrast, are exogenous.
options: Alkylation
Reactive oxygen species (ROS)
DNA glycosylase
Mismatch repair (MMR)
questions.why: Endogenous mutagens come from replication errors and ROS; exogenous ones include UV (which causes pyrimidine dimers), ionising radiation (which causes double-strand breaks) and intercalating agents. The other options are a chemical change to a base, a repair enzyme, and a repair pathway.

questions.q: DNA damage produced when the cell is attacked by external factors (for example ultraviolet light or ionising radiation) falls into which class?
options: endogenous
Direct reversal
exogenous
somatic recombination
questions.why: Exogenous mutagens include UV, ionising radiation and intercalating agents; the endogenous ones come from replication errors and ROS. The other options are the class of damage arising inside the cell, a repair mode that excises nothing, and the recombination that builds receptor diversity in somatic cells.

questions.q: A gene knock-in has to insert a foreign sequence precisely into the target gene, so it must be given a ______ and be completed through the HR pathway.
options: donor template
gRNA
PAM
Ku
questions.why: A knock-in needs both a donor template and HR (only available in S/G2, when sister chromatids exist) for a precise insertion; a knock-out instead relies on NHEJ producing indels to disrupt the gene. The other options are the guide RNA, the adjacent-sequence requirement for Cas9 to cut, and the protein that caps the DNA ends in NHEJ.

questions.q: When CRISPR/Cas9 is used to “knock out” a gene, it is the cell's own ______ repair mechanism that joins the two ends back together, incidentally leaving a few bases of insertion or deletion.
options: Homologous recombination (HR)
Mismatch repair (MMR)
Nucleotide excision repair (NER)
Non-homologous end joining (NHEJ)
questions.why: A knock-out goes through NHEJ: it needs no template and is error-prone, and the indels it produces often cause a frameshift that renders the gene non-functional; HR is the high-fidelity route. The other choices are the template-dependent repair, the repair of replication mismatches, and the repair of bulky lesions.

questions.q: The difference between “GG-NER (global genome repair)” and TC-NER lies in which protein performs the first step of GG-NER, scanning the whole chromosome?
options: XPA: slides along DNA and only stops where it meets a distortion
XPC: patrols the whole genome and recognises the damaged segment
TFIIH: opens the double helix over a short stretch first
CSA and CSB: brought in by the transcription complex with the repair machinery
questions.why: The first step of global genome repair is XPC patrolling the whole chromosome and recognising that a stretch of DNA “does not look right”; TC-NER is instead handled by CSA and CSB on the strand being transcribed. The other choices describe the protein that positions the excision machinery, the helicase complex that opens the DNA, and the proteins summoned by the stalled transcription complex.

questions.q: In CRISPR/Cas9, which piece of RNA is responsible for bringing Cas9 to the target DNA sequence?
options: PAM
HNH
gRNA
RuvC
questions.why: gRNA is the guide RNA: it base-pairs with the target DNA and delivers Cas9 there; RuvC and HNH are Cas9's own two nuclease domains. The other options are the adjacent-sequence requirement for Cas9 to cut and the two nuclease domains that cut each strand.

questions.q: After the DNA of HBV integrates into the host genome, what observation about tumour prognosis follows?
options: The more integration sites there are, the significantly worse the patient's survival
After integration the virus can no longer make RNA
Integration methylates the host DNA throughout
Integration is unrelated to prognosis and is merely a by-product of viral replication
questions.why: The figure the lecturer quotes is: three or more integration sites → significantly worse survival, so HBV integration sites can serve as a prognostic marker. The other choices describe a block on viral RNA production, wholesale methylation of the host DNA, and integration as a meaningless by-product of replication.

questions.q: What is the role of the “Helper T cell” in the immune response?
options: The cytotoxic T cell that directly kills infected cells
The antigen-presenting cell that cuts the antigen into peptides and presents them to T cells
The B cell that makes antibodies directly
The helper T cell that helps B cells produce antibodies and activates macrophages and other immune cells
questions.why: Helper T cells (CD4) receive the antigen signal through MHC class II and then secrete cytokines that assist B cells and macrophages; beyond antibody diversity, the quantity of antibody also depends on them. The other choices describe the cytotoxic T cell, the antigen-presenting cell and the antibody-producing B cell.

questions.q: One of Cas9's two nuclease domains, the one that cuts the DNA strand paired with the gRNA, is called what?
options: RuvC
HNH
PAM
TFIIH
questions.why: Cas9's HNH cuts the target strand (the one paired with the gRNA) and RuvC cuts the other strand; together they create the double-strand break next to the PAM. The other options are the nuclease domain that cuts the other strand, the adjacent-sequence requirement for cutting, and the helicase complex of NER.

questions.q: What characterises “Homologous recombination (HR)”?
options: It requires a homologous template, runs in S/G2, and repairs precisely without easily going wrong
It cuts out only a single damaged base, which DNA polymerase then puts back
It needs no template, can run in any phase of the cell cycle, but readily leaves indels behind
It excises a bulky lesion of 22–32 nucleotides and then resynthesises
questions.why: HR needs a template (the sister chromatid) and is available only in S/G2, so it repairs precisely; NHEJ needs no template, works in every phase, but is error-prone. This contrast is the pair most likely to be turned into a question. The other choices describe the repair of a single damaged base, the template-free but error-prone end joining that leaves indels, and the excision of a bulky lesion.

questions.q: When HR runs in S/G2, the cell uses the homologous DNA of the ______ (the sister chromatid) as a template to rejoin the broken ends correctly.
options: homologous template
donor template
gRNA
PAM
questions.why: HR's template is the cell's own homologous DNA — the sister chromatid in S/G2; the donor template used for a knock-in is separately supplied donor DNA, and comes from a different source. The other options are the guide RNA and the adjacent-sequence requirement for Cas9 to cut.

questions.q: What characterises “Homology-directed repair”?
options: It joins the broken ends directly through NHEJ, regardless of whether the sequence is correct
It runs only in G1, leaving unrepaired damage for the next cell cycle
It methylates the DNA throughout so that it cannot be transcribed
It uses homologous recombination to graft the sequence from the template precisely onto the target position
questions.why: HDR is the precise route: homologous recombination inserts the new sequence, so a knock-in needs both a template and S/G2; the NHEJ route is fast but error-prone. The other choices describe the template-free end joining that ignores sequence correctness, a G1-only repair, and the DNA methylation that blocks transcription.

questions.q: In DNA repair and gene editing, what does an indel refer to?
options: An inversion of a large segment of a chromosome
A small insertion or deletion
Both strands of the DNA breaking at the same time
A base mismatch on the newly synthesised strand
questions.why: An indel is a small insertion or deletion: when NHEJ joins the broken ends back together it often leaves a few bases gained or lost, and if that falls in the coding region and causes a frameshift it is the mechanism of gene knock-out. The other choices are a large chromosomal inversion, a double-strand break and a replication mismatch.

questions.q: In the context of this chapter, what does “integration” mean?
options: DNA polymerase adding new nucleotides to the 3′ end of the old strand
RNA polymerase moving along DNA and synthesising mRNA
Viral DNA integrating into the host genome, for example the integration sites of HBV
A ribosome translating mRNA into a polypeptide chain
questions.why: The number of HBV integration sites correlates with survival (three or more → significantly worse survival), so integration is treated in this lecture as a prognostic marker. The other choices describe DNA synthesis, transcription and translation.

questions.q: The first step of NHEJ is the work of the Ku heterodimer (Ku70/Ku80); what is its function?
options: Recognising and protecting the DNA ends so that they are neither resected nor annealed
Carrying out recombination using the sister chromatid as a template
Patrolling the whole genome and marking the positions of damaged chromosomes
Cutting the DNA ends in order to create a double-strand break
questions.why: Ku is the first step of NHEJ: it caps and protects the DNA ends, and DNA-PKcs then joins to form the DNA-PK complex; V(D)J recombination borrows them, so a defect causes SCID. The other choices describe the template-driven recombination, the genome-wide patrol for damage, and the nuclease that makes the break in the first place.

questions.q: What is the division of labour between “KU and DNA-PKcs” in NHEJ?
options: Both are DNA polymerases, responsible for putting the missing nucleotides back
Both are nucleases, responsible for cutting on either side of the broken end
Both are downstream effectors of p53, responsible for starting apoptosis
Ku protects the DNA ends, DNA-PKcs is the kinase associated with it, and the two together form the core mechanism of NHEJ
questions.why: Ku and DNA-PKcs form the DNA-PK complex, which is the core of NHEJ; V(D)J recombination borrows them to join the V, D and J segments, so a defect causes severe immunodeficiency. The other choices describe the polymerase that fills the gap, the nucleases that make the cuts, and the apoptotic effectors downstream of p53.

questions.q: Which molecular system displays the processed antigen peptides on the cell surface for T cells to recognise?
options: TCR (T-cell receptor)
MHC (major histocompatibility complex)
Antibody
DNA glycosylase
questions.why: MHC is the molecule for “display”: class I presents to CD8 and class II to CD4; TCR and antibodies are on the side that recognises the antigen. The other options are the recognising molecules and the enzyme that excises a damaged base in BER.

questions.q: MHC class I presents endogenous antigens to CD8 ______, so that it can recognise infected or otherwise damaged cells.
options: Helper T cell
B cell
T-cell
Antigen-presenting cell
questions.why: Class I presents endogenous antigens to CD8 T cells, whereas class II presents exogenous antigens to CD4 helper T cells — this is the cleanest point of distinction. The other options are the CD4 cell that receives exogenous antigen, the cell that makes the antibodies, and the cell that loads peptides onto MHC.

questions.q: Which class of antigen does “MHC class II” present, and to which class of T cell?
options: Exogenous antigens presented to CD4 helper T cells
Endogenous antigens presented to CD8 cytotoxic T cells
Endogenous antigens presented to CD4 helper T cells
Exogenous antigens presented to CD8 cytotoxic T cells
questions.why: Class II specifically presents exogenous antigens to CD4 helper T cells; class I is the one that presents endogenous antigens to CD8. The other choices are the three combinations that the class I/II distinction rules out.

questions.q: Short tandemly repeated sequences (STR), where the same locus can have different lengths within a population, are called ______.
options: Indel
Mismatch repair (MMR)
Ku
Microsatellite
questions.why: A microsatellite is a short repeat of a few nucleotides; replication is prone to slippage there, so its length changes, and MMR is the pathway responsible for tidying up those changes. The other options are the small insertion or deletion, the repair pathway for those changes, and the protein that caps the DNA ends in NHEJ.

questions.q: When a cell's mismatch repair (MMR) fails, the repeat lengths in microsatellite regions change at random; what is this phenomenon called?
options: MMR deficiency
Microsatellite instability (MSI)
Mismatch repair (MMR)
Polymerase slippage
questions.why: MMR cannot repair the mismatches caused by slippage during replication, so the number of microsatellite repeats gradually changes — this is MSI; MSI-H tumours therefore carry many neoantigens and become hot tumours. The other options are the failure of the repair system itself, the pathway that normally fixes the changes, and the slipping event that creates them.

questions.q: Which class of error is “Mismatch repair (MMR)” responsible for repairing?
options: A multi-nucleotide bulky lesion damaged by ultraviolet light
A single base that has been alkylated
Bases mismatched between the newly synthesised strand and the old strand, together with the small insertions and deletions that arise during replication
Both strands of the whole DNA breaking at once
questions.why: MMR repairs the mismatches and small loops that arise after replication; bulky lesions are the business of NER, a single base is BER, and double-strand breaks are handled by HR or NHEJ. The other choices are the ultraviolet bulky lesion, the chemically altered single base and the break of both DNA strands.

questions.q: What role does “Mlh1” play in mismatch repair (MMR)?
options: A key MMR factor (paired with PMS2) that takes over once a mismatch has been recognised and organises the excision and resynthesis
A protein that slides along DNA, finds the damaged position and assembles the excision enzymes there
The nuclease domain of Cas9 that cuts the strand paired with the gRNA
The protein that patrols the whole genome to find the damaged position
questions.why: MLH1 and PMS2 form one set of the MMR machinery and take over once a mismatch has been recognised; the other set, responsible for recognising the mismatch, is MSH2/MSH6. The other choices describe the protein that positions the excision machinery in NER, the Cas9 nuclease domain that cuts the gRNA-paired strand, and the genome-wide patrol for damage.

questions.q: What special clinical significance do MMR-deficient tumours have?
options: They become cold tumours and therefore do not respond to immunotherapy
They are always MSS and have nothing to do with immunotherapy
They completely disable HR, so the patients need PARP inhibitors
They are mostly MSI-H with many neoantigens, are hot tumours, and respond well to checkpoint inhibitors such as anti-PD-1
questions.why: MMR deficiency → many frameshift mutations → a high neoantigen burden → hot tumour → a response to anti-PD-1; the lecturer quotes that about 15% of colorectal cancers are MSI-H. The other choices describe the cold-tumour opposite, the MSS state that has nothing to do with immunotherapy, and the loss of HR that makes tumours sensitive to PARP inhibitors.

questions.q: In the classification of tumour immunity, what are MSI-H (microsatellite instability-high) tumours called?
options: cold tumour
hot tumour
MMR deficiency
SCID (severe combined immunodeficiency)
questions.why: MSI-H and MMR deficiency → many neoantigens → hot tumour → a good response to checkpoint inhibitors; the lecturer calls the survival curve of dMMR versus pMMR one of the most important graphs in modern medicine. The other options are the cold-tumour opposite, the state of the failed repair system, and the severe immunodeficiency caused by an NHEJ defect.

questions.q: Most colorectal cancers are not MSI-H but ______; they have few neoantigens, are cold tumours, and respond poorly to checkpoint inhibitors.
options: Microsatellite instability (MSI)
MMR deficiency
MSS
Homologous recombination (HR)
questions.why: MSS is the situation in which mismatch repair is intact; only the small MSI-H/MMR-deficient group (the lecturer quotes about 15%) are hot tumours that respond to anti-PD-1. The other options are the instability itself, the failure of the repair system, and the template-dependent repair of double-strand breaks.

questions.q: What characterises “Non-homologous end joining (NHEJ)”?
options: It needs no template, can run in any phase of the cell cycle, but repairs in an error-prone way and leaves indels behind
It requires a homologous template, runs in S/G2, and repairs precisely
It excises a stretch of 22–32 nucleotides containing a bulky lesion
It repairs the base mismatches between the newly synthesised strand and the old strand after replication
questions.why: NHEJ is fast but error-prone; V(D)J recombination borrows it to assemble receptor segments and CRISPR uses it for knock-outs; its deficiency is SCID. The other choices describe the template-dependent repair that is accurate, the excision of a bulky lesion, and the repair of replication mismatches.

questions.q: What characterises “Nucleotide excision repair (NER)”?
options: It cuts out only a single damaged base, which DNA polymerase then puts back
It joins the two ends of the DNA together without needing a template
It finds the mismatches in the newly synthesised strand after replication and corrects them
It excises a stretch of 22–32 nucleotides, removing the bulky lesion in its entirety
questions.why: XPF and XPG make the cuts on either side of the damaged fragment in NER, releasing a stretch of 22–32 nucleotides; the fixed size of the gap is the clue the lecturer uses to distinguish NER from the other pathways. The other choices describe the repair of a single damaged base, the template-free joining of broken ends, and the correction of replication mismatches.

questions.q: When DNA damage is severe and cannot be repaired, what role does p53 play in the cell?
options: It excises the damaged base directly from the DNA
It triggers cell-cycle arrest and apoptosis, so that the damaged cell stops dividing
It separates the two strands of the DNA being replicated
It is the variable region of an antibody light chain
questions.why: DSB → ATM → p53 is the backbone of the damage response: p53 decides whether the cell repairs, pauses its division, or moves towards apoptosis. The other choices describe the enzyme that excises a damaged base, the separation of DNA strands and a component of the antibody.

questions.q: In CRISPR/Cas9, what does “PAM” refer to?
options: The guide RNA that brings Cas9 to the target DNA position
The nuclease domain that cuts the strand paired with the gRNA
The adjacent sequence that must sit next to the target sequence for Cas9 to cut, which limits where Cas9 can act
The nuclease domain that cuts the other strand
questions.why: PAM is the protospacer adjacent motif: the gRNA decides which stretch is cut and the PAM decides whether the cut can be made here; both are indispensable. The other options are the guide RNA and the two nuclease domains that cut each strand.

questions.q: Why are PARP inhibitors especially effective against BRCA-mutant tumours?
options: BRCA mutations disable HR, so the tumour cells depend on PARP for repair; inhibiting PARP kills them, while normal cells can still survive on HR
It inhibits Cas9 directly, so it works only on cells that are being gene-edited
It blocks NHEJ, and so causes SCID
It reduces DNA methylation and thereby suppresses all gene expression
questions.why: This is synthetic lethality: BRCA mutation → HR deficiency; a PARP inhibitor then closes the other route, leaving the tumour cell with nowhere to go, while normal cells survive on intact HR, which gives a wide therapeutic window. The other choices describe the blocking of Cas9, the blocking of NHEJ and a reduction in DNA methylation.

questions.q: What does “polymerase slippage” mean?
options: The polymerase adds the wrong nucleotide, which an exonuclease later corrects
The polymerase adds nucleotides to the wrong end, reversing the direction
The polymerase stalls on damaged DNA, setting off the DNA damage response
DNA polymerase slips during replication, so the template is copied with a few bases too many or too few
questions.why: Slippage gives repeat sequences (microsatellites) one extra or one fewer copy; if MMR cannot repair it, the changes accumulate into MSI. The other options describe a misincorporated nucleotide, the addition of nucleotides to the wrong end, and the stalling of the polymerase on damaged DNA.

questions.q: What is the most typical bulky lesion caused by ultraviolet light hitting DNA?
options: AP site
pyrimidine dimers
Mismatch repair (MMR)
Non-homologous end joining (NHEJ)
questions.why: UV cross-links adjacent pyrimidines into dimers, distorting the double helix, so the whole stretch has to be excised by NER before it can be repaired. The other options are the base-less position left by DNA glycosylase, the repair pathway for mismatches, and the template-free end joining of broken ends.

questions.q: What is the role of “RAD51” in homologous recombination?
options: The nuclease that excises bulky lesions
The protein that slides along DNA to localise the damage for NER
The core HR protein that wraps single-stranded DNA into a nucleofilament and promotes homologous pairing and invasion
The MMR factor that recognises replication mismatches and organises their excision
questions.why: RAD51 is the engine of HR: it wraps the single-stranded DNA released from RPA into a nucleofilament and promotes homologous invasion; RAD52 assists RAD51 in loading onto the DNA. The other choices describe the nuclease that removes bulky lesions, the positioning protein of NER, and the MMR factor that recognises replication mismatches.

questions.q: At the first step of HR, what are RPA and RAD52 each doing?
options: RPA first stabilises the exposed single-stranded DNA by binding to it, and RAD52 helps RAD51 replace RPA and form the nucleofilament
RPA separates the two strands of DNA and RAD52 joins the two strands back together
RPA cuts the DNA and RAD52 supplies the missing nucleotides
RPA attaches the DNA to the chromosome and RAD52 anchors it to the nuclear membrane
questions.why: RPA holds the single-stranded DNA so that it cannot re-anneal or be attacked by nucleases; RAD52 brings RAD51 in and swaps RPA for a RAD51 nucleofilament, and only then does homologous invasion properly begin. The other choices describe the separation and rejoining of strands, the cutting and resynthesis of DNA, and the attachment of DNA to the chromosome and nuclear membrane.

questions.q: In the classification of DNA damage, which class of mutagen does “Radiation” belong to, and what damage does it cause?
options: An endogenous mutagen: ionising radiation causes oxidation of bases
An exogenous mutagen that joins adjacent pyrimidines into dimers
An endogenous mutagen that directly forms DNA adducts
An exogenous mutagen: ionising radiation causes double-strand breaks in DNA
questions.why: Exogenous mutagens include UV (which causes pyrimidine dimers), ionising radiation (which causes double-strand breaks) and intercalating agents; the endogenous ones come from replication errors and ROS. The other choices are the endogenous class with its oxidative or adduct-forming damage, and the exogenous class that makes pyrimidine dimers.

questions.q: What do the reactive oxygen species (ROS) produced during cellular metabolism do to DNA?
options: Both strands of the DNA break at the same time
They cause endogenous oxidative damage, for example oxidising bases — a routine source of DNA damage
They cause pyrimidine dimers
They cause bulky lesions that remove a whole stretch of DNA
questions.why: ROS is an endogenous source of oxidative stress that oxidises bases (most typically 8-oxoG); most of these small chemical changes are repaired by BER, and those that are not become fixed as mutations. The other choices are the double-strand break, the pyrimidine dimer and the bulky lesion removed as a whole stretch.

questions.q: What role do “recombination-signal sequences (RSS)” play in antibody diversity?
options: The variable-region sequences of the antibody heavy chain
The molecular sequences responsible for presenting antigen to T cells
The signal sequences at the two ends of the V, D and J segments, which pull the segments together and hand them to the recombination machinery
The short tandem repeat sequences found within microsatellites
questions.why: V(D)J recombination uses the RSS at the two ends of the segments (12-RSS and 23-RSS) to pull V, D and J together, and then borrows NHEJ to join them; the segment copy numbers V ≈ 39, D = 27 and J = 6 determine the diversity. The other choices describe the variable region of the heavy chain, the antigen-presenting sequences and the short repeats of microsatellites.

questions.q: TC-NER is called “transcription-coupled excision repair” precisely because of what RNA polymerase does when it meets damage on DNA:
options: It stalls on the damaged DNA and summons the repair machinery to that spot on the spot
It skips over the damage and keeps transcribing without stopping
It excises the stretch of DNA that contains the damage
It switches to another template and carries on transcribing
questions.why: The term “transcription-coupled” says it all: what is damaged is the strand being transcribed, and the RNA polymerase stalling there is the signal to start; CSA and CSB are the genes of this pathway. The other choices describe the skipping of the damage, the excision of the damaged stretch and the switch to another template.

questions.q: Which kind of RNA is “RNA polymerase II” responsible for transcribing?
options: Messenger RNA (mRNA)
Ribosomal RNA (rRNA)
Transfer RNA (tRNA)
The mitochondrion's own RNA
questions.why: RNA polymerase II transcribes mRNA, so the expression of protein-coding genes is coupled to transcription; the TC-NER arm of NER is started precisely because the transcription complex halts on the damage. The other options are the messenger RNA, the ribosomal RNA and the transfer RNA.

questions.q: In DNA repair, which protein first protects the single-stranded DNA exposed after the break, acting as a “single-stranded DNA binding protein”?
options: RAD51
RPA
XPC
Ku
questions.why: RPA binds the single-stranded DNA first, preventing it from re-annealing or being attacked by nucleases; RAD52 then helps RAD51 replace it with a nucleofilament. The other options are the protein that forms the nucleofilament, the protein that patrols the genome for damage in GG-NER, and the protein that caps the DNA ends in NHEJ.

questions.q: Of Cas9's two nuclease domains, the one that cuts the “non-target strand” is ______; the other, HNH, cuts the strand paired with the gRNA.
options: HNH
PAM
RuvC
TFIIH
questions.why: Cas9's HNH cuts the target strand and RuvC cuts the other; the two domains together create the double-strand break next to the PAM. The other options are the domain that cuts the gRNA-paired strand, the adjacent-sequence requirement for cutting, and the helicase complex of NER.

questions.q: In the context of this chapter, how does “SCID (severe combined immunodeficiency)” arise?
options: An NHEJ defect prevents the diversity of antibodies and TCRs from being built up, so both cellular and humoral immunity are lost
An MMR defect turns the tumour into a hot tumour
An HR defect makes the patient especially sensitive to PARP inhibitors
An NER defect means the dimers caused by ultraviolet light cannot be excised
questions.why: The causal chain is: NHEJ is borrowed by V(D)J recombination to assemble V + D + J → this generates the diversity of antibodies and TCRs → an NHEJ defect therefore becomes severe immunodeficiency. The other choices describe defects of MMR, HR and NER and their consequences.

questions.q: In the DNA damage response, what is the job of the “sensors”?
options: Excising the damaged stretch of DNA directly
Carrying out proofreading during DNA replication
Sliding along DNA to position the repair machinery at the damaged site
Recognising the damage that occurs on DNA and passing the signal to the downstream signalling and execution molecules
questions.why: The lecturer describes the damage response in three stages, sensors → transducers → effectors: the sensors (ATM, ATR) detect the damage first, the signal travels downwards, and the effectors finally decide whether to repair or to kill. The other choices describe the excision of the damage, the proofreading of replication and the positioning of the repair machinery.

questions.q: In the immune system, the recombination that takes place within somatic cells during the development of B and T cells (as distinct from the exchange of homologous chromosomes at meiosis) is called what?
options: branch migration
somatic recombination
Nucleotide excision repair (NER)
Direct reversal
questions.why: Somatic recombination occurs during the development of somatic cells (B and T cells) and generates receptor diversity through V(D)J recombination; meiotic recombination happens when gametes are formed, with a different purpose and timing. The other options are the step of HR that extends the paired region, the repair of bulky lesions and the repair mode that excises nothing.

questions.q: What does “Synthetic lethality” mean in tumour therapy?
options: Two mutations cancel each other out, so the cell returns to normal
A single drug attacks several targets at once and the toxicities add up
The cell dies only when two defects that are each harmless on their own occur together, which is why the therapeutic window is wide
The cell stops growing in a hypoxic environment
questions.why: A BRCA mutation (HR deficiency) together with a PARP inhibitor is synthetic lethality: neither alone is lethal, but combined the tumour cell dies, while normal cells survive on intact HR. The other choices describe two mutations cancelling each other out, one drug with several targets and the arrest of growth in hypoxia.

questions.q: V(D)J recombination serves two receptor systems: antibodies in B cells, while the TCR is in ______; the diversity of both is built by the same NHEJ route.
options: T-cell
Helper T cell
Antigen-presenting cell
Mismatch repair (MMR)
questions.why: The V(D)J recombination of the T-cell receptor is exactly the same as that of antibodies, so an NHEJ defect knocks out the capability on both the T-cell and the B-cell side. The other options are the CD4 cell, the cell that loads peptides onto MHC, and the repair pathway for replication mismatches.

questions.q: What is the full name of “TC-NER”, and what is the scope of what it handles?
options: Global genome NER: it repairs only the regions that are not being transcribed
Transcription-coupled MMR: it corrects base mismatches in the newly synthesised strand
Transcription-coupled BER: it repairs a single alkylated base
Transcription-coupled NER: it gives priority to excising damage on the strand of DNA that is being transcribed
questions.why: The dividing line between TC-NER and GG-NER is “where the damage is looked for”: TC-NER acts where the transcription complex has stalled on the damage, whereas GG-NER has XPC scan the whole chromosome. The other choices are the global-genome arm of NER and the transcription-coupled forms of MMR and BER.

questions.q: Which molecule do T cells use to recognise the “MHC–peptide” complex?
options: MHC (major histocompatibility complex)
TCR (T-cell receptor)
Antibody
Antigen-presenting cell
questions.why: TCR is the recognising side and MHC the presenting side; together they decide whether the T cell recognises the antigen, and this is also why TCR diversity has to be built by V(D)J recombination. The other options are the presenting molecule, the antibody and the cell that loads the peptides.

questions.q: What role does “TFIIH” play in the DNA damage response?
options: It is the positioning protein of NER, sliding along DNA to look for the damage
It is the protein that scans the whole genome in GG-NER
It contains a DNA helicase that first opens the double helix over a short stretch, so that repair enzymes can reach the damaged DNA
It is the nuclease domain of Cas9
questions.why: The first step of NER is TFIIH using its helicase to open a short stretch of DNA; XPA then positions the machinery and XPF and XPG make the cuts on either side. The other choices describe the positioning protein, the genome-wide scanner and the Cas9 nuclease domain.

questions.q: What does “Therapeutic window” mean in drug development?
options: The margin between the effective dose and the toxic dose; the larger the gap, the wider the safe range over which the drug can be used
The time from dosing until the patient shows a response
The time the drug takes to reach its highest concentration in the blood
The number of targets a single drug can act on at the same time
questions.why: The lecturer uses the therapeutic window to explain the benefit of synthetic lethality: tumour cells and normal cells differ in their sensitivity to the same drug, and once that difference is widened, normal cells stay within the safe range. The other choices describe the time to a response, the time to peak concentration and the number of targets.

questions.q: What does “tolerance” mean in immunology?
options: The process by which T cells begin to proliferate after receiving antigenic stimulation
The immunodeficiency caused by insufficient antibody diversity
The ability of antigen-presenting cells to cut the antigen into peptides
The state in which the immune system fails to respond to certain antigens, including self-antigens
questions.why: Tolerance is the state of “not responding”: the immune system stays silent towards self-antigens or long-standing antigens; it is the exact opposite of SCID, where all defence is lost. The other choices describe the proliferation of T cells after stimulation, the immunodeficiency of too little antibody diversity and the processing of antigen into peptides.

questions.q: He divides the signalling chain of the DNA damage response into three stages: sensors sense the damage, ______ pass the signal downwards, and effectors carry out the response.
options: Effectors
Transducer
Sensors
RPA
questions.why: Sensors → transducers → effectors is a top-down division of labour: the sensors detect the problem, the transducer passes on the signal, and the effector alone decides between repair, arrest and apoptosis. The other options are the final executing stage, the sensing stage and the single-stranded DNA binding protein of HR.

questions.q: What DNA damage does “Ultraviolet light” cause?
options: Both strands of the DNA break at the same time
Bases being alkylated
A bulky lesion in which adjacent pyrimidines are joined as dimers, which has to be excised as a whole stretch by NER
A mismatch in the newly synthesised strand after replication
questions.why: UV is an exogenous mutagen that causes pyrimidine dimers; such bulky lesions are exactly what NER acts on, and this is the pair most often used to ask about BER versus NER. The other choices are the double-strand break, the chemical alteration of a base and the replication mismatch.

questions.q: If the NHEJ pathway cannot operate, the cell cannot complete V(D)J recombination, and the result will be ______.
options: SCID (severe combined immunodeficiency)
MMR deficiency
MSI-H
therapeutic window
questions.why: NHEJ deficiency → no antibody or TCR diversity can be built up → severe immunodeficiency (SCID); this causal chain is the one the lecturer explicitly marks as a question type. The other options are the failure of mismatch repair, the state of high microsatellite instability and the margin between effective and toxic doses.

questions.q: What is the function of “XPA” in NER?
options: Patrolling the whole genome to find DNA segments that “do not look right”
Making the cuts on either side of the damaged fragment, releasing 22–32 nucleotides
Opening a short stretch of DNA so that other enzymes can get close
Moving along DNA like a sliding clamp, stopping only where it finds a distortion and positioning the excision machinery at the damaged site
questions.why: Positioning in NER is the job of XPA; XPC handles the genome-wide scan, TFIIH opens the DNA, and XPF and XPG make the cuts — the division of labour between these four roles is what this pair tests. The other choices describe the genome-wide scan, the making of the cuts and the opening of the DNA.

questions.q: In nucleotide excision repair, which protein patrols the whole chromosome, recognises the damaged segment, and must also avoid the DNA that is being replicated?
options: XPA
XPC
TFIIH
XPF and XPG
questions.why: The first step of global genome repair is the XPC patrol; only after it has identified the damaged position are XPA, RPA and XPF/XPG called in. The other options are the positioning protein, the helicase complex that opens the DNA, and the two endonucleases that make the cuts.

questions.q: What is the role of “XPF and XPG” in NER?
options: Both are positioning proteins that assemble the repair machinery in place
Both are helicases that open the DNA
Two endonucleases that cut on either side of the damaged fragment, releasing 22–32 nucleotides
Both are DNA polymerases that fill in the gap
questions.why: The excision in NER is carried out by XPF and XPG, and the 22–32 nucleotides released are the evidence that “a stretch of DNA damage has been removed in its entirety”, and also the clue the lecturer uses to distinguish NER from the other pathways. The other choices describe the positioning proteins, the helicases and the polymerases that fill the gap.

questions.q: Which older, protein-based method of cutting DNA at a chosen site was superseded by CRISPR/Cas9 because it is far more expensive to design?
options: ZFN
gRNA
PAM
TFIIH
questions.why: A ZFN is a protein-based nuclease in which each unit recognises DNA with a zinc finger, so designing one means re-engineering the protein; CRISPR/Cas9 replaces the whole protein recognition module with a short gRNA, which is far cheaper to design. The other options are the guide RNA, the adjacent-sequence requirement for Cas9 to cut and the helicase complex of NER.
